props.title: The North Avenue Irregulars

sections.content: Disney's **The North Avenue Irregulars (1979)** (1979) stands as a fascinating entry in the late 1970s family action-comedy genre, blending church politics with vigilante justice in an unexpectedly engaging way. The film follows Edward Herrmann as Reverend Michael Hill, who recruits a group of church women to help the Treasury Department take down local mobsters. It shares DNA with other female-led crime-fighting comedies like **9 to 5** (1980) and **Private Benjamin** (1980), but adds a unique suburban church twist. The film's greatest strength lies in its ensemble cast, including Barbara Harris and Cloris Leachman, who bring genuine chemistry and comedic timing to their roles as unlikely crime fighters.

sections.content: The film represents a specific moment in Disney's live-action filmmaking when the studio was attempting to modernize its family entertainment formula. Like **Freaky Friday** (1976) and **The Cat from Outer Space** (1978), it aimed to capture contemporary audiences while maintaining Disney's wholesome brand. Director Bruce Bilson, known for television work including **Get Smart**, brings a sitcom-style pacing that keeps the action moving while never letting the stakes feel too dangerous for family viewing.

What makes **The North Avenue Irregulars** (1979) particularly noteworthy is its treatment of female characters. While still operating within 1970s constraints, it presents its church ladies as capable, intelligent individuals who rise to the occasion rather than mere comic relief. This approach predates later films like Sister Act (1992) and **Calendar Girls** (2003), which similarly featured unlikely groups of women taking on unexpected challenges. sections.content: The film sits at an interesting crossroads between Disney's earlier live-action comedies like **The Love Bug** (1968) and their more modern approach that would emerge in the 1980s. The car chase sequences and undercover operations show clear influence from popular crime comedies of the era like **Smokey and the Bandit** (1977), but filtered through Disney's family-friendly lens. This hybrid approach would influence later Disney productions like **Honey, I Shrunk the Kids** (1989) and **Three Men and a Baby** (1987).
